8
A mass is placed on a frictionless slope inclined at 30° to the horizontal. The mass is then
released.
What is its acceleration down the slope?
A
4.9 m s–2
B
5.7 m s–2
C
8.5 m s–2
D
9.8 m s–2

hints: Notice the slope is frictionless at $30^{\circ}$ to the horizontal, so the only force pulling the mass down the slope is part of its weight.
Recall weight $mg$ acts vertically down, so its component parallel to the slope involves $\sin 30^{\circ}$, not full $g$ or $\cos 30^{\circ}$.
Set resultant force $ma$ equal to $mg \sin 30^{\circ}$ and cancel $m$ to find $a = g \sin 30^{\circ}$ with $g = 9.8 \text{ m s}^{-2}$.
walkthrough: Identify the motion: mass $m$ on a smooth $30^{\circ}$ slope, so no friction and the normal force has no component along the slope.
State the driving force: weight $W = mg$ acts vertically down, and the component along the slope is $W_{\text{parallel}} = mg \sin \theta$.
Apply Newton's second law down the slope: $F = ma$, so $ma = mg \sin 30^{\circ}$ and mass $m$ cancels to give $a = g \sin 30^{\circ}$.
Substitute $g = 9.8 \text{ m s}^{-2}$ and $\sin 30^{\circ} = 0.5$: $a = 9.8 \times 0.5 = 4.9 \text{ m s}^{-2}$ down the slope.

A.explanation: Resultant force down the frictionless slope is $mg \sin 30^{\circ}$, so $a = g \sin 30^{\circ} = 4.9 \text{ m s}^{-2}$.

B.explanation: This is $g \tan 30^{\circ}$, which incorrectly uses tangent instead of the parallel component $g \sin \theta$.

C.explanation: This is $g \cos 30^{\circ}$, which is the perpendicular component pressing into the slope, not the component pulling down the slope.

D.explanation: This is full $g$, which would apply in vertical free fall, not when weight is resolved along a $30^{\circ}$ slope.
